answers.reasoning: Nora commands Helmer to sit and listen; calm, firm, deliberate, reversing their usual dynamic. Not sarcastic, pleading, or playful.
Metaphorical reckoning of wrongs in the marriage, not literal finances or a gentle reconciliation.
She reframes eight years as never having been a true partnership of serious exchange.
Helmer assumes worries are his domain and Nora couldn't help bear them—she's unfit to share serious matters.
'Dearest Nora' plus doubt it would do her any good = affectionate condescension.
Helmer claims to have loved her best; Nora says he only thought it pleasant to be in love with her—dispute over whether his enjoyment of the role is love of her.
Her uncertainty shows conformity has blurred the line between her real self and her role.
Doll-child transferred from papa's hands to Helmer's: love as possession denying her a self. Other options overreach or contradict the text.
'Come to the window' places the speaker indoors addressing a nearby companion.
'Only... Listen!' introduces the 'grating roar' that brings 'the eternal note of sadness in,' disturbing the tranquil visual scene.
Faith 'was once... at the full' like a girdle round the earth; 'But now' only its 'withdrawing roar' retreating.
'Naked shingles of the world' extends the metaphor: the world stripped bare as faith's covering (girdle) withdraws.
'Let us be true to one another! for the world... hath really neither... certitude' — love as the sole refuge.
Seems a land of dreams; really has neither joy, love, light, etc. — appearance hides emptiness.
Speaker urges 'let us be true' yet says the world has 'neither joy, nor love' — the tension between love's plea and love's denial.
'Ignorant armies clash by night' is a metaphorical image of blind conflict confirming the bleak worldview; no resolution or return to calm.
The withdrawing 'sea of faith' and the appeal to be true to one another support the thesis of lost faith with personal fidelity as the only consolation.
'Improved' is ironic: Sir Walter's additions (daughter's marriage, wife's death date) serve his vanity; narrator mocks his sense that he enhances the record.
The reader sees him poring over his own entry and annotating it before the narrator states 'Vanity was the beginning and the end'—showing before telling.
A new-made lord's valet is delighted with borrowed, fresh status; the comparison deflates Sir Walter's pride as servile and unrefined.
'The Sir Walter Elliot, who united these gifts, was the constant object of his warmest respect and devotion'—he reveres himself.
The narrator corrects 'legacy' to 'charge': the daughters are a responsibility entrusted to 'a conceited, silly father', not property.
The narrator comments knowingly on the public's unreasonable attitudes to widows remarrying—a worldly, sociable commentator.
The parenthesis reveals he was rejected in unreasonable proposals, undercutting his 'prided himself on remaining single for his daughters' sake'.
He would give up anything—but hasn't been tempted to, so the sacrifice is untested, ironically hollow.

Ironic praise ('like a good father', 'improved') exposes vanity; Anne's 'elegance of mind and sweetness of character' is affirmed though she is 'only Anne'. Option 0 wrong since Anne does not share vanity.
Every planned item (shoes, shirt waists, gown, stockings, caps, hats) is for the children; the 'little brood looking fresh' excites her. No hint of self-spending or resentment.
'dim' = vague, 'monster' = menacing, 'sometimes appalled' + 'to-morrow never comes' = kept at a distance; not constant terror.
The remark is a wry consolation—tomorrow of course does come; the irony is that she only postpones her dread.
Faint, tired, hungry: physical weakness makes her receptive to the soothing silk and the impulse that follows.
Military diction (charge, besieging, breastworks) frames bargain shopping as combat requiring force and endurance, matching the earlier elbowing and clutching.
'soft, sheeny luxurious,' 'glisten,' 'glide serpent-like' convey tactile pleasure, with the serpent suggesting temptation.
'Hectic blotches' in pale cheeks = feverish flush of excitement as desire rises.
'Pretended' signals that the careful-examination pose covers an already-formed impulsive desire.
The exclamation and the parcel 'lost in the depths of her shabby old shopping-bag' convey how slight and easily concealed the purchase is, contrasting with the bulging money earlier.
She abandons the bargain counter's crowd for a 'retired corner' where she privately changes into the silk stockings and revels in them.
Third-person omniscient access to her mind reveals an action that bypasses her own reasoning; no first-person shift, no harsh condemnation.
She forgot to eat lunch because she was feeding the children and righting the place—direct evidence of neglecting herself for the family.

The passage moves from selfless planning for the children to unthinking sensuous indulgence, suggesting that long self-denial yields to a buried hunger for pleasure. Other theses overreach (moral ruin, documentary, scheming).
'Begin and cease, and then again begin' uses repetitive, cyclical syntax conveying endless monotonous recurrence that brings the 'eternal note of sadness.'
Sophocles heard the same note 'long ago' on the Aegean; 'we / Find also' by this 'distant northern sea' — sadness shared across ages and places.
'Ebb and flow' is literally tidal motion and figuratively the recurring rise and fall of 'human misery'; 'turbid' is not soothing, and no prediction of ending.
The world 'seems' like a land of dreams, 'so various, so beautiful, so new,' but 'really' has no joy, love, light — appealing promise that is illusory.
Stanza 1 present scene, stanza 2 Sophocles/ancient past, stanza 3 sea of faith, stanza 4 returns to address the lover ('Ah, love'). No dawn, no hopeful resolution, ending is not tranquil.

He admires the 'limited remnant of the earliest patents' and feels contempt for the 'almost endless creations of the last century'—regard keyed to age and rarity of titles, not scholarship or balance.
'To them he must have owed a wife of very superior character to any thing deserved by his own'—only looks and rank could have won her; his character itself had nothing to recommend it.
Humoured, softened, concealed his failings: she managed and compensated for his faults rather than sharing them; nothing suggests hostility or shame in public.
Not the happiest, but duties, friends, children attached her to life—measured contentment despite the marriage.

Vanity of person and situation is his core; Elizabeth being handsome and like himself means she mirrors him, hence her influence. The other daughters are 'of very inferior value', ruling out equal regard.

'Apparently... but really' marks the narrator's access to her inner 'speculation and calculation' beneath the outward dreamy appearance. Narrator is third person, not Mrs. Sommers; no doubt about plans is expressed.
'She herself indulged in no such morbid retrospection... The needs of the present absorbed her every faculty.' No grief, hope, or resentment is stated.

Her hand rests 'aimlessly' on the counter and 'by degrees she grew aware' of something soothing—chance, tactile discovery, not planned or skillful; the clerk merely asks, after she has already touched them.

Earlier she deliberated for days; the stockings are bought on impulse with 'hectic blotches,' and later 'She was not thinking at all... abandoned herself to some mechanical impulse.' No conscious ranking; she counts money fine (hands over five dollars, waits for change).

Stockings first appear as a thrifty family purchase saving darning; later the same item becomes a sensual luxury for herself ('How good was the touch of the raw silk'). No regret stated; silk is not cheaper than cotton.
